title: Residence or actual power?

knows: Selected accounts can describe distinct institutions and dated changes.
doesNotKnow: Timurid, Safavid and Mughal court relationships, separating court presence from control

objective: Timurid, Safavid and Mughal court relationships, separating court presence from control

claims.text: In Safavid Herat, resident princes could hold nominal governorship while military hakems exercised government; Shamlu commanders became effectively hereditary, and Aliqoli Khan challenged central authority in 1577–88.
Aliqoli Khan’s challenge and 1588–1598 Uzbek interruption are retained; prince residence does not equal effective central rule.

claims.text: Iranica distinguishes Herat’s nominal princely governor from effective military commanders and challenges to central power, including an Uzbek interruption. TDV describes Kabul’s governors after Babur’s court moved to Agra. Residence, nominal title and working administration are different relations. Uncollated originals and qualified retrospectives establish neither continuous homogeneous control nor identical powers at both cities.
